division.heading: Lawyers’ Charges, Retainer Agreements and Right of Review

operative_text.controlling:
10.14(1)  If a lawyer is served with notice of an appointment for
a review of the lawyer’s charges or retainer agreement, or both,
the lawyer must file
(a) a copy of the account, appropriately signed, in respect of
which the client seeks a review,
(b) a copy of any time records upon which the account is
based, and
(c) a copy of any retainer agreement between the lawyer and
the client whether or not the lawyer intends to rely on
them.
(2)  The documents must be filed 5 days or more before the
appointment date or within any other period specified by a review
officer, and the review officer may vary the period before or after
the time limit has passed.
(3)  If the lawyer does not comply with this rule, the lawyer forfeits
the right to payment of the lawyer’s charges in any account that is
the subject of a review unless the review officer otherwise directs.

BOOK_A.title: Client-Obtained Appointment: Lawyer’s Responsibility
BOOK_A.operative_text_raw:
10.14(1) If a lawyer is served with notice of an appointment for a review of the
lawyer’s charges or retainer agreement, or both, the lawyer must ﬁle
(a) a copy of the account, appropriately signed, in respect of which the
client seeks a review,
(b) a copy of any time records upon which the account is based, and
(c) a copy of any retainer agreement between the lawyer and the client
whether or not the lawyer intends to rely on them.
(2) The documents must be ﬁled 5 days or more before the appointment date or
within any other period speciﬁed by a review ofﬁcer, and the review ofﬁcer may
vary the period before or after the time limit has passed.
(3) If the lawyer does not comply with this rule, the lawyer forfeits the right to
payment of the lawyer’s charges in any account that is the subject of a review
unless the review ofﬁcer otherwise directs.¹
[Alta. Reg.124/10;140/13;128/15;36/20]
BOOK_A.commentary:
The "forfeiture" in subrule (3) should not be mechanical and automatic, and sometimes a
very brief adjournment may enable production of the missing information, in which case the fault
should be excused.²
If a party seeks costs, especially full-indemnity costs, it must provide at the beginning of the
review by a review ofﬁcer a bill of costs, a statement of account, or other evidence of the amounts
claimed.³
A client objecting to his or her lawyer’s bill must give particulars of the objections.⁴

(1) If a lawyer is served with notice of an appointment for a review of the lawyer’s charges or retainer agreement, or both, the lawyer must file (a) a copy of the account, appropriately signed, in respect of which the client seeks a review, (2) The documents must be filed 5 days or more before the appointment date or within any other period specified by a review officer, and the review officer may vary the period before or after the time limit has passed.
(3) If the lawyer does not comply with this rule, the lawyer forfeits the right to payment of the lawyer’s charges in any account that is the subject of a review unless the review officer otherwise directs.

commentary.text:
In assessing whether they should exercise their discretion to protect a lawyer from forfeiture under rule 10.14, the review officer should consider whether a short adjournment would remedy the issue.An adjournment could be as short as a few minutes. The review officer should balance potential prejudice to the client with providing them the basic tools needed to determine whether the lawyer’s account was reasonable. Moore v. Hildebrand, [2013] A.J. No. 270, 2013 ABQB 167 at para. 22 (Alta. Q.B.).
The foundational rules (Part 1) cannot override the specific requirement in rule 10.14 to file a retainer agreement. Moore v. Hildebrand, [2013] A.J. No. 270, 2013 ABQB 167 at para. 16 (Alta. Q.B.). The quickest way at the least expense for the review officer to get background context for a fee dispute is to examine, before the review hearing, the basic materials, including the retainer agreement, that will establish the right to recovery. Moore v. Hildebrand, [2013] A.J. No. 270, 2013 ABQB 167 at para. 17 (Alta. Q.B.).
